BOPEN.heard: Building virtual environments exam prep, key terms, concept art and character art. 34 terms for game art from what makes a picture clear, to how concept art narrows ideas, to how a sculpt becomes a model the engine can run. Exact terms turn a vague art request into when you can check.

BIDEA.heard: Hollow, this is Liam in For Bear. Newcomers often say concept art is the finished art of a game. It is not. Concept art is early rough drawing that solves a design problem for the team and its polish hardly matters. Game art is full of lookalike terms like that. This film goes through them group by group, each one shown, so you can name the exact one.

BDEFS.heard: Seven labels sit in the corners of the pictures that follow. In the book text, the course text uses and explains the term. In the glossary, the term is on the course term list, but the text does not explain it. Video only, the term comes from a video lecture and is not in the course text or on the term list. Computed, the numbers are worked out on screen from stated inputs. Simulation, a model run step by step from stated rules, not a measurement of a real game. Illustrative data, numbers chosen to show the idea, not measured. Conceptual, a drawing of the idea with no data behind it.

B0101.heard: This table is the map 34 art terms in four groups. The first group is what art must do with clarity, satisfaction, art style and pushed proportions. These are the jobs game art has and the look it sets.

B0102.heard: The second group is Steering the Eye. Visual hierarchy, contrast in its kind, light and dark, color, shape and size, then silhouette, shape language, area of focus, rest in high detail, and atmospheric perspective. These decide what a player sees first.

B0103.heard: The third group is concept art. Concept art itself reference mood board, the constraint in its three kinds, thematic perspective and mechanics, then ideation, two-tone sketching, closing doors and iteration. These are how early designs are found and narrowed.

B0104.heard: The fourth group is character art, iconic elements, proxy model, readability, high-poly sculpt, low-poly mesh, UV map and unwrapping, texture baking, anatomy and neutral pose. These take a design all the way to a character in the game.

B0201.heard: Eight things drawn at game size. Clarity means the player can tell at once what is happening, who is friend or foe and where to go. In this made-up example, a thing counts as readable at 16 pixels or more in 3 to 1 contrast and only 4 of the 8 pass. For example, a spiked trap drawn in the same brown as the floor fails Clarity because the player sees the danger only after landing on it.

B0202.heard: Satisfaction means each action gets a quick responsive answer, so acting feels good. Both squares answer the same press. In this made-up example, the fast one answers in 40 milliseconds and the slow one in 700-660 later and it lags. Clarity asks whether you can tell what is going on. Satisfaction asks whether it feels good to act. For example, a coin that pops and chimes the instant the player touches it is satisfying.

B0203.heard: Art style is the consistent look of a game, its color, its designs, and its shapes. These two pictures share the same shapes and layout. Only the color use differs. A mean saturation of 0.81 against 0.11 and the scene feels quite different. For example, if your game is flat pixel art in a small, bright palette, every new enemy in coin must follow that choice or it looks out of place.

B0204.heard: Push proportions or shapes exaggerated on purpose as in a cartoon look. The three figures share one body and the red head grows from 14% of the height about realistic to 22 than 33. For example, a player character drawn with an oversized head and short legs reads as a cartoon on purpose, not as a realistic person.

B0301.heard: Six circles and a bar for each. Visual hierarchy means arranging a picture so the most important things are seen first than the next in order. Your attention is scored as size times contrast, a simple stand-in. The boss gets 46%, the player 22, the rock only 3. Contrast is one difference and hierarchy is the order the eye visits. For example, on a title menu the start button should be seen first, the options next. And the credits last.

B0302.heard: Contrast is any difference that pulls the eye to one place and it can be measured. Three color pairs sit on a scale from 1 to 21. White on cream is 1.111 almost invisible. Dark ink on cream is 11.23 to 1 and black on white is 21 to 1. For example, a white score number on a pale sky is hard to see and a dark outline around it raises its contrast.

B0303.heard: Light and dark contrast is the gap between light and dark areas with hue taken away. Each color on top is shown below as its gray. Red and blue look very different, yet both land at 0.13 almost the same gray. Light and dark contrast survives a black and white copy and color alone often does not. For example, turn a level screenshot gray. If a red enemy in a blue floor become one gray, make the enemy much lighter or darker.

B0304.heard: Color contrast means strong differences in color or saturation, how pure color is. In each row one circle is the odd one. In the top row it's saturation is 0.76 among circles at 0.07 and it jumps out. In the bottom row the gap is only 0.13 and it hides. For example one bright gold key in a gray stone room is found at once.

B0401.heard: Two rows of seven shapes, shape and size contrast means one thing differs in size or outline from the rest so it is seen first or it points the way. In the top row one circle is twice the median size. In the bottom row one shape has three corners and the other six have none. For example an exit door far taller than the small crates around it is spotted the moment the player enters the room.

B0402.heard: Silhouette is the outline of an object alone, and it should still say what the object is when filled black at game size. A knight and a blob are filled black and shrunk from 48 down to 6. The telepart score is 1 minus their overlap and it stays between 0.42 and 0.53 at every size. For example, fill a new enemy sprite black beside the player, add its size in the level, and check you can still name it.

B0403.heard: Now the knight sits beside a near copy, the same outline with small differences. At 48 the telepart score is only 0.06 and by 6 it is 0. The two outlines have become 1. Small details vanish as a silhouette shrinks. For example, two enemies that differ only by a belt buckle look like the same enemy at game size, so give one of them a different overall outline.

B0404.heard: Shape language is how the forms of a design express its personality or idea. Three forms are measured by their sharpest corner, rounded at 165 degrees blocky at 90 spiky at 25. The number only describes the form and what it says is the artist's choice. Shape and size contrast is about standing out, shape language is about meaning. For example, you give a friendly shopkeeper soft, round shapes, and a boss sharp spikes. And keep that rule across the whole game.

B0501.heard: A checkerboard with one black square in the middle. Area focus is the place in an image where the artist wants the eye to land. The center against its neighbor is 7.9 to 1. The outer neighbors are only 2.4 to 1, so the eye goes to the center. For example, on the last screen of a level, the exit door can be the area of focus. The one spot the art steers the player toward.

B0502.heard: Rest in high detail means leaving plain regions beside a busy one, so the busy part reads as important. In this made-up example, both rows spend the same 64 strokes, spread evenly, the focus tile holds 13%. Concentrated with rest around it, it holds 67%. Area focus is where the eye should land, and rest is what makes it land there, for example. Keep a level's floor tiles plain, and spend the detail on the one carved door the player must find.

B0503.heard: Atmospheric perspective means far away things lose detail and contrast, which adds depth and guides the eye. Six trees stand farther and farther to the right. With a made-up fall-off, their contrast drops from 100% to 17, and their detail lines thin out. For example, in a side-scrolling level, you paint the Far Mountains pale and plain and the near trees dark and detailed, so the player knows what is only background.

B0601.heard: A scatter of 40 sketches, concept art is early drawing that solves a design problem for the team, not finished art. In this simulated set, the red dot solved three or four problems, fifteen of the forty. Polish tells you almost nothing, a correlation of 0.01. For example, a page of rough sketches that each try a different way to show where a jumping enemy will land is concept art, even if none is clean.

B0602.heard: Reference means real world images and examples gathered to research a subject before drawing. Here in this simulated set, 24 images are gathered, three groups of eight from different places. Reference is any image you gather. A mood board is a chosen set that shows the tone. For example, before drawing a termite enemy, you collect photos of real termites, their jaws, their legs, and the way they stand, and you note where each photo came from.

B0603.heard: A mood board is a set of reference images that shows the theme and tone shown to the team early. From the same 24, two boards of six are chosen. The ink dots are a narrow board with a spread of 31 pixels. The red rings are scattered 218 about seven times wider. The narrow one points the team one way. For example, six pictures of dim, wet caves pinned together set the tone for an underground level.

B0701.heard: 60 dots stand for 60 ideas in this simulated set. A constraint is a limit that narrows what the artist designs, with no limit all 60 stay open and nothing says which way to go. A constraint narrows the design and reference is images gathered for research. For example, telling the agent their new enemy may use only the few palette colors the player uses is a constraint on its design.

B0702.heard: A thematic constraint is a limit that comes from the game's lore, setting and tone. Here the thematic limit turns 29 ideas hollow, ideas that do not fit the world and 31 stay open. For example, a game set inside an underground termite colony rules out shiny robots and spaceships, however good they look.

B0703.heard: A perspective constraint is a limit that comes from the player's view, first person, third person, or top down. The view limit shuts 13 more ideas and 18 stay open. For example, Walker is seen from the side, so the termite reference which shows the creatures from above may not fit a side view level without a new drawing.

B0704.heard: A mechanics constraint is a limit that comes from the game's rules and numbers, such as an ability or a health total. The rules limit shuts 7 more, and 11 of the 60 ideas are left. For example, if an enemy is defeated when the player jumps on its head, its design needs a clear top the player can see and land on.

B0801.heard: 24 rough thumbnails. Ideation means making many quick rough ideas before choosing one. Drawing fast and loose gets the idea across without polish. In this made-up example, each sketch takes about 5 seconds, so all 24 take 120 seconds. For example, before asking for a final coin sprite, you fill a page with quick coin shapes, stars, gems and rings, and only then pick one.

B0802.heard: Two-tone sketching means sketching in only two colors, so you cannot fuss over small detail. In full color, this picture has 11 colors to decide. In two tones, it has two, and only the big shapes stay in view. For example, block out a new level's background in just dark and light first, and add color only once the big shapes work.

B0803.heard: Closing doors means each round shuts the options that failed and they are not reopened. Each row is one round. Twenty-four ideas become twelve, then six, then three, keeping the better half each time. Closing doors drops whole options and iteration reworks the one that is kept. For example, once the team drops the flying version of an enemy, nobody brings it back at the next review.

B0804.heard: Iteration means repeating a cycle of draft, feedback and change. The line is the gap to what the team needs. In this simulated run it shrinks from 1.00 to 0.04 over 5 cycles. Show work early, not in one grand reveal. For example, you show a rough jump animation to a plate ester. Hear that the landing feels stiff, change it and show it again.

B0901.heard: Seven features of one character ranked. Iconic elements are the few features that keep a character recognizable even when tiny on screen. In this made up example a feature shows only if its thinnest side is at least three pixels. The pauldron the shoulder armor survives down to 27 pixels, the sword and scarf to 32. The buckle needs 96. For example, if your hero is known by a red scarf. Draw the scarf big enough to show when the hero is small and let tiny buckles go.

B0902.heard: A proxy model is a rough block model of the big shapes used to check proportions and silhouette early. The black blocks are the proxy and the dashed red outline is the target. Over three rounds of correction the size error falls from 19% to 2%. For example, before anyone sculpts a new enemy in Blender, you stack three boxes for its head, body and legs, and check its height beside the player in Go-Doh.

B0903.heard: Readability is how well a character can be understood in the game's real view. One character is drawn at three sizes, at 200 pixels all seven features show, at 64, 6 of 7, at 32 only three. Silhouette is the outline alone and readability is the whole character at its real size. For example, judge a new enemy sprite in the running game next to the player, not zoomed in inside an image viewer.

B1001.heard: A circle the outline of a very smooth sphere. A high poly sculpt is a very detailed model, shaped like clay, holding all the detail and far too heavy for the engine. This sphere has 1,046,528 triangles, more than a game can draw in real time. For example, a character sculpted in Blender with every wrinkle and scale in its mesh is a high poly sculpt and it stays in Blender.

B1002.heard: A low poly mesh is a simplified copy of the sculpt with far fewer polygons, light enough for the engine to run. The red sphere has 16 sides and 224 triangles, 4,672 times fewer. Its edges off by 1.9% so the silhouette holds but the detail is gone. For example, the model you export from Blender into Godot is the low poly mesh, not the sculpt.

B1003.heard: The UV map named for the two axes of a flat image is the flat layout of a model's surface used to place a texture. Unwrapping is the cutting that makes it. A cube has six faces and twelve edges. Cut seven, the red dashes keep five joined and it lies flat as a cross, each face with a place to paint. For example, in Blender you mark seams down the back of a character's coat, unwrap it and paint the coat on the flat image.

B1004.heard: Texture baking stores the sculpt's detail as an image on the low poly mesh. The top row is how light shades the bumpy high poly surface. The flat low poly misses the bumps off by 0.37. With the baked image it is off by only 0.04. For example, you bake the wrinkles of a high poly boot into a normal map, so the low poly boot and go-dough still looks wrinkled.

B1101.heard: A two-bone arm reaches for six targets from a shoulder on the left. Anatomy means knowing how bones and muscles work so a sculpt looks believable and can be animated. The jointed limb with an elbow reaches five of the six targets. A rigid bar of the same length reaches one. The gray target is out of range. For example, give a spider enemy knee joints in the right places, and its walk animation can bend each leg naturally.

B1102.heard: The neutral pose is the default pose a model is built in, and some designs that look right in it fail once the character moves. Each arm is raised from that pose until a shoulder plate blocks it. The heavy plate stops it at 96 degrees and the trimmed plate at 107. Anatomy is how the body works, the neutral pose is how it stands while built. For example, a knight with huge shoulder armor may look fine standing. One cannot raise its sword overhead to attack.

B1201.heard: Each pair sets two look alike terms side by side. Contrast is a difference between two things, like this pair at 11.2 to 1. Visual hierarchy is the order in which many things are seen first, second, third and fourth.

B1202.heard: Reference is any image gathered for research. Here 12 spread over 110 pixels. A mood board is a narrow chosen set that sets the tone. Here five images, tight and on theme.

B1203.heard: A proxy model is rough blocks to check proportions, three blocks size only. A low-poly mesh is the light copy of a sculpt that the engine runs, 16 sides and 224 triangles. The proxy comes before the sculpt, the low-poly after it.

B1204.heard: Silhouette is the outline alone filled black here 24 by 24. Readability is whether the character is understood in the game's real view, as it shrinks seven of seven features show then six then three.

B1301.heard: A vague request sits above the exact instruction that replaces it, beside a chart of what it does. Make the enemy pop becomes, raise the enemy against the floor from 1.2 to 1, to at least 3 to 1, 4.2 to 1 passes.

B1302.heard: Make the hero readable becomes, fill the silhouette black at 24 pixels and keep its telepart score from the enemy above 0.30. Against the blob it scores 0.44. The near copy at 0.06 fails.

B1303.heard: Draw the eye to the hero becomes put at least 60% of the detail budget on the focal tile. 43 of 64 is 67%. Spread evenly, it is 13% and only the concentrated tile passes.

B1304.heard: The mood is all over the place becomes choose six images within 60 pixels of their center. The narrow board spreads 31 pixels and passes. The scattered set spreads 218 and does not.

B1305.heard: I cannot pick when idea becomes drop the weaker half each round 24 12 6 3 and never reopen a door once it is closed. 24 ideas become 3 and 3 rounds.

B1401.heard: This is a checklist of six questions to ask before you call a piece of art ready. First, can a player tell what is happening at once and does the game answer each action? That is clarity, then satisfaction.

B1402.heard: Second, where does the eye land first and is that the most important thing on screen that is visual hierarchy and the area of focus?

B1403.heard: Third, fill the silhouette black at the size it has in the game. Does the shape still say what it is, and can it be told apart from its neighbors?

B1404.heard: Fourth, which constraint does this design solve and what reference is it built on. Concept art exists to solve a problem, so name the problem.

B1405.heard: Fifth, did you show the work early and ask a specific question about the goal? That is iteration, not a grand reveal at the end.

B1406.heard: 6. Does the character hold up at the size it has in the game's real view? That is readability. Then say it exactly a number, a size, a limit, not make it better.

BVDT.heard: Let's recap, Clarity is telling what is going on and satisfaction is feeling good to act. Contrast is one difference, and visual hierarchy is the order the eye visits. A silhouette must still say what it is, filled black at game size. Concept art solves a design problem and its polish hardly matters. Constraints narrow the ideas and closing doors drops the weaker ones each round. A high poly sculpt's detail is baked onto the low poly mesh the engine runs.

BHTF.heard: Quizmy on game art terms with short game-making cases one at a time. Use the terms clarity, satisfaction, visual hierarchy, contrast, silhouette, readability, reference, mood board, proxy model, and low poly mesh. For each case I must name the exact term and say why its look alike is wrong. Hold back the answer until I reply, then tell me if I was right.

BOUT.heard: Key terms concept art and character art at Nick Bear Brown.
